questions.s: A 58-year-old man in Multan has had poorly controlled hypertension for 15 years. Echocardiography shows a thick-walled left ventricle with normal chamber size. Which cellular adaptation explains the increased ventricular mass?
questions.e: Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot divide, so a sustained pressure load is met by an increase in the size of each cell (hypertrophy) through more contractile proteins. Hyperplasia needs cells that can enter the cell cycle, which adult myocytes essentially cannot.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has had heartburn for over ten years. Endoscopic biopsy from the lower oesophagus shows columnar epithelium containing goblet cells where squamous epithelium is expected. Which process does this represent?
questions.e: Replacement of one adult cell type by another (here squamous by intestinal-type columnar epithelium in Barrett oesophagus) is metaplasia, an adaptation to chronic acid injury. Dysplasia means disordered growth with cytological atypia; it may develop later within the metaplastic epithelium but is not what is described.

questions.s: A 67-year-old woman dies three weeks after an ischaemic stroke. At autopsy the infarcted area of the left cerebral hemisphere is soft and partly cystic, filled with lipid-laden macrophages. Which type of necrosis is seen?
questions.e: Hypoxic death in the central nervous system produces liquefactive necrosis because brain tissue is rich in lipid and poor in structural protein, so enzymatic digestion dominates and leaves a cystic cavity. Coagulative necrosis, where cell outlines persist, is the pattern of infarcts in solid organs such as heart and kidney.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man with heavy alcohol use dies of severe acute pancreatitis. At autopsy there are multiple chalky white foci in the peripancreatic and omental fat. What is the basis of these foci?
o: Enzymatic fat necrosis with calcium soap formation
Caseous necrosis due to tuberculous peritonitis
Fibrinoid necrosis of small mesenteric arteries
Dry gangrene of the omentum after vessel thrombosis
questions.e: Lipases released from injured acinar cells split triglycerides in adjacent fat, and the released fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky white soaps (saponification). Caseous necrosis looks cheesy and is typical of tuberculosis, not of enzymatic injury around the pancreas.

questions.s: A coronary artery is occluded in an experimental model and myocardial cells are examined by electron microscopy at intervals. Which ultrastructural finding indicates that the injury has become irreversible?
o: Small lipid droplets in the cytoplasm
Detachment of ribosomes from the endoplasmic reticulum
questions.e: Large flocculent (amorphous) densities in mitochondria, together with severe membrane damage, mark the point of no return in ischaemic injury. Cellular swelling, fatty change and ribosome detachment are features of reversible injury and recover if blood flow is restored.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has acute hepatitis B with ALT of 1,450 U/L. A liver biopsy shows scattered shrunken, intensely eosinophilic hepatocytes with dense nuclear fragments, lying singly without surrounding inflammation. What is this form of cell death?
questions.e: Single shrunken eosinophilic cells with condensed or fragmented chromatin and no inflammatory reaction are apoptotic bodies (Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis), produced by cytotoxic T cells activating caspases. Coagulative necrosis affects groups of cells, causes swelling rather than shrinkage and provokes inflammation.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman in Rawalpindi is brought 30 hours after swallowing a large number of paracetamol tablets. Her ALT is 6,200 U/L. What is the main mechanism of hepatocyte injury?
o: Depletion of glutathione by a reactive metabolite
Direct inhibition of mitochondrial ATP synthase
Antibody-mediated destruction of hepatocytes by complement
questions.e: In overdose, paracetamol is increasingly metabolised by cytochrome P450 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, which uses up glutathione and then binds cell proteins, causing centrilobular necrosis. This is why acetylcysteine, which replenishes glutathione, is the antidote; immune mechanisms play no primary part.

questions.s: A 75-year-old man has severe aortic stenosis. The excised valve shows nodular calcium deposits within the cusps. His serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL (8.5-10.5) and parathyroid hormone is normal. What type of calcification is this?
questions.e: Calcium deposited in damaged or degenerated tissue with normal serum calcium is dystrophic calcification, typical of aged and damaged heart valves. Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues when serum calcium is raised, for example in hyperparathyroidism.

questions.s: At autopsy, an 85-year-old woman has a small brown heart. Microscopy shows yellow-brown granules around the myocyte nuclei that do not stain with Prussian blue. What is the pigment?
questions.e: Lipofuscin is the wear-and-tear pigment of lipid peroxidation that accumulates around nuclei in ageing cells, giving brown atrophy of the heart and liver. Haemosiderin is iron-derived and stains blue with Prussian blue, so a negative stain excludes it.

questions.s: A 16-year-old boy has an appendicectomy 12 hours after the onset of abdominal pain. Histology of the appendix wall shows an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the muscularis propria. Which cell type predominates?
questions.e: Neutrophils dominate the infiltrate in the first 6-24 hours of acute inflammation, and their presence in the muscle wall confirms acute appendicitis. Macrophages replace them after 24-48 hours, while lymphocytes and plasma cells characterise chronic inflammation.

questions.s: A 3-week-old boy has omphalitis and the umbilical cord stump is still attached. His white cell count is 38 x 10^9/L, mostly neutrophils, yet there is no pus at the site of infection. Which molecule is most likely defective?
questions.e: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 is caused by defective CD18, the beta-2 integrin subunit needed for firm adhesion of neutrophils to endothelium, so neutrophils stay in the blood (marked neutrophilia), cannot reach tissues to form pus, and cord separation is delayed. NADPH oxidase defects (chronic granulomatous disease) impair killing but neutrophils still migrate and abscesses form.

questions.s: A 7-year-old girl with typhoid fever has a temperature of 39.8 °C and is given ibuprofen, after which her fever settles. Inhibition of which mediator in the hypothalamus mainly explains the effect on fever?
questions.e: Pyrogenic cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF induce cyclooxygenase in the hypothalamus, and the resulting prostaglandin E2 raises the temperature set point. NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase and so reduce fever; leukotriene B4 is a lipoxygenase product and is not affected by NSAIDs.

questions.s: A gardener in Faisalabad is stung by a wasp. Within minutes a raised red wheal forms, which subsides within half an hour. What is the main mechanism of the fluid leak in this immediate response?
o: Direct necrosis of endothelium in arterioles and capillaries
questions.e: Histamine released from mast cells causes rapid, short-lived contraction of endothelial cells in postcapillary venules, opening gaps through which fluid leaks; this is the immediate transient response. Direct endothelial necrosis follows severe injury such as burns and causes a sustained leak from all vessel types.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has right lower lobe pneumonia with a pleural effusion. The aspirated fluid is cloudy, with protein 4.2 g/dL and many neutrophils. Which mechanism mainly produced this fluid?
questions.e: A protein-rich, cellular fluid is an exudate, which forms when inflammation increases vascular permeability so that plasma proteins and leukocytes escape. Raised hydrostatic pressure and low oncotic pressure produce a transudate with low protein, as in heart failure or nephrotic syndrome.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman from Peshawar has a matted cervical lymph node. Biopsy shows granulomas with central caseation. Which cytokine, secreted by Th1 cells, is chiefly responsible for activating macrophages into epithelioid cells?
questions.e: In tuberculosis, IL-12 from macrophages drives Th1 cells to secrete interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages, transforming them into epithelioid cells and giant cells that form granulomas. IL-4 and IL-5 are Th2 cytokines, and IL-10 dampens macrophage activation.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with untreated chronic kidney disease and a blood urea of 220 mg/dL has a pericardial friction rub. He dies, and at autopsy both pericardial surfaces are rough and shaggy with a yellow-grey coating. What type of inflammation is this?
questions.e: Uraemic pericarditis is a classic fibrinous inflammation: larger vascular leaks allow fibrinogen to escape and form fibrin on the serosa, giving a bread-and-butter appearance and a friction rub. Serous inflammation produces a thin, protein-poor fluid without a shaggy coat, and suppurative inflammation produces pus.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman with septic arthritis has a C-reactive protein of 180 mg/L. Which cytokine is the main stimulus for hepatic synthesis of this protein?
questions.e: CRP, fibrinogen and serum amyloid A are acute-phase proteins whose hepatic production is driven mainly by IL-6 (with IL-1 and TNF). IL-8 is a neutrophil chemokine and does not drive hepatic protein synthesis.

questions.s: Which arachidonic acid metabolite is a potent chemoattractant for neutrophils in acute inflammation?
questions.e: Leukotriene B4, made by the lipoxygenase pathway, is a powerful neutrophil chemotactic and activating agent. Leukotriene C4 belongs to the cysteinyl leukotrienes, which cause bronchospasm and increased permeability rather than chemotaxis.

questions.s: A 22-year-old woman had her earlobe pierced a year ago. She now has a firm, shiny, rubbery mass at the site that has grown well beyond the margins of the original wound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A keloid is an excess of collagen that extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound and tends not to regress; it is more common in darker skin. A hypertrophic scar is also raised but stays within the wound margins and often flattens with time.

questions.s: A 62-year-old diabetic man has a leg ulcer whose base is red, granular and bleeds easily on touch. What would histology of this ulcer base show?
o: Proliferating fibroblasts and new thin-walled capillaries
Epithelioid macrophages forming multinucleate giant cells
Dense acellular bundles of type I collagen
questions.e: Granulation tissue is the hallmark of healing: new capillaries (angiogenesis) and proliferating fibroblasts in a loose oedematous matrix, which gives the red, granular, easily bleeding surface. Dense acellular collagen is the later scar, and epithelioid giant cells indicate granulomatous inflammation.

questions.s: A 70-year-old widower living alone eats almost no fruit or vegetables. He has swollen bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and a surgical wound that has failed to heal. Which step of collagen synthesis is impaired?
o: Incorporation of glycine into the chain
questions.e: Vitamin C is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases; without hydroxylation, collagen triple helices are unstable, giving scurvy with fragile vessels and poor wound healing. Lysyl oxidase needs copper, not vitamin C, and acts on the later cross-linking step.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has a clean sutured laparotomy wound. Approximately what proportion of the tensile strength of normal skin does the scar reach by about three months?
questions.e: When sutures are removed at about a week, wound strength is around 10 % of normal skin; it rises steeply over the next weeks and plateaus at about 70-80 % by three months. A scar does not regain the full strength of unwounded skin, which is why incisional hernias can occur.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man had an anterior myocardial infarction three months ago. What would histology of the infarcted area now show?
questions.e: Cardiac myocytes are permanent cells that cannot regenerate, so the infarct heals by fibrosis, and by about two months it is largely a dense collagen scar. Granulation tissue dominates at about 1-2 weeks, and neutrophils with coagulative necrosis are seen in the first few days.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has taken prednisolone for rheumatoid arthritis for several years. After a hysterectomy her wound remains weak and gapes on suture removal. How do glucocorticoids mainly impair wound healing?
o: Increased platelet aggregation in the wound
questions.e: Glucocorticoids suppress inflammation and inhibit TGF-beta production, reducing fibroblast activity and collagen deposition, so the scar is weak. They reduce, not enhance, neutrophil migration into tissues.

questions.s: A large sacral pressure ulcer in a bedbound man heals over several weeks by secondary intention, and its area shrinks markedly before epithelium covers it. Which cell is mainly responsible for this wound contraction?
questions.e: Myofibroblasts are modified fibroblasts with smooth-muscle-type actin that pull the wound edges together, a key feature of healing by secondary intention. Macrophages orchestrate healing by releasing growth factors and clearing debris but do not themselves contract the wound.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man donates the right lobe of his liver to his brother. Within a few weeks his remaining liver has nearly regained its original volume. How are adult hepatocytes classified by their proliferative capacity?
o: Stable cells that are normally quiescent but can divide
Permanent cells that cannot re-enter the cell cycle
Terminally differentiated cells replaced only from bone marrow
questions.e: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent) cells: they normally rest in G0 but re-enter the cell cycle after loss of tissue, which explains regeneration after partial hepatectomy. Labile cells such as surface epithelia and haematopoietic cells divide continuously throughout life.

questions.s: A 48-year-old woman is ten days into her recovery from a hip fracture repair and has been mostly in bed. She suddenly becomes breathless, collapses and dies. Autopsy shows a large embolus straddling the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk. Where did this embolus most likely originate?
o: A mural thrombus in the right atrium
An atheromatous plaque in the carotid artery
A mural thrombus in the left ventricle
The deep veins of the leg
questions.e: Over 95 % of pulmonary emboli arise from thrombi in the deep veins of the legs, favoured here by immobility and orthopaedic surgery (stasis and endothelial injury of Virchow's triad). Left ventricular and carotid sources embolise to the systemic circulation, not the lungs.

questions.s: At autopsy, a thrombus attached to the wall of an abdominal aortic aneurysm shows alternating pale layers of platelets and fibrin and darker layers of red cells. What do these laminations indicate?
o: Thrombus formed in flowing blood before death
Clot formed in static blood after death
Septic embolus from an infected heart valve
Thrombus that has been fully recanalised
questions.e: Lines of Zahn are alternating platelet-fibrin and red-cell layers that form only in flowing blood, so they distinguish an antemortem thrombus. Postmortem clots are gelatinous, unattached, and show a dark red lower part with a yellow chicken-fat upper part, without laminations.

questions.s: A 23-year-old motorcyclist has a closed fracture of the femoral shaft. Forty-eight hours later he becomes breathless and confused, with oxygen saturation of 86 % on air and petechiae over the chest and axillae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: The triad of respiratory distress, neurological change and petechial rash appearing 1-3 days after a long-bone fracture is fat embolism syndrome, caused by marrow fat globules lodging in the microcirculation. Pulmonary thromboembolism usually occurs later and does not produce a petechial rash.

questions.s: After occlusion of an artery, which organ typically develops a red (haemorrhagic) infarct rather than a pale one?
questions.e: Red infarcts occur in loose tissues with a dual blood supply, such as the lung (pulmonary and bronchial arteries), where blood continues to flow into the necrotic area. Solid organs with end-arterial supply, such as kidney, spleen and heart, develop pale (white) infarcts.

questions.s: A 65-year-old woman with rheumatic heart disease has had right heart failure for years. At autopsy the cut surface of the liver shows a mottled pattern of dark red areas alternating with paler tan areas. What is the main microscopic finding?
o: Macrovesicular fatty change around portal tracts
Portal tract granulomas with giant cells
questions.e: Chronic passive congestion from right heart failure dilates the central veins and sinusoids around them, with atrophy or necrosis of centrilobular hepatocytes, giving the nutmeg liver. Regenerative nodules with bridging fibrosis describe cirrhosis, which only develops after very prolonged severe congestion.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has a chronic cough. Sputum cytology shows many alveolar macrophages filled with golden-brown granules that stain blue with Prussian blue. What do these cells indicate?
questions.e: Mitral stenosis raises pulmonary venous pressure, causing small alveolar haemorrhages; macrophages ingest the red cells and store the iron as haemosiderin, forming heart failure cells. Tuberculosis and abscess produce inflammatory cells and necrosis rather than iron-laden macrophages.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman with acute pyelonephritis has blood pressure 80/40 mmHg, a bounding pulse of 124/min and warm, flushed peripheries. What is the main mechanism of her hypotension at this stage?
o: Reduced cardiac output from myocardial infarction
Systemic vasodilation caused by inflammatory mediators
Obstruction to venous return to the heart
questions.e: Early septic shock is a distributive shock: microbial products trigger cytokines and nitric oxide that dilate peripheral vessels, so the skin is warm and cardiac output may even rise. Hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock cause cold, clammy peripheries from compensatory vasoconstriction.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has swelling around the eyes in the morning and generalised oedema. Urine dipstick shows protein 4+ and serum albumin is 1.6 g/dL (3.5-5.0). What is the main mechanism of his oedema?
questions.e: Heavy urinary protein loss in nephrotic syndrome lowers serum albumin, reducing plasma oncotic pressure so fluid moves into the interstitium. Increased permeability produces protein-rich exudates in inflammation, not generalised oedema with hypoalbuminaemia.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman develops a deep vein thrombosis three months after starting a combined oral contraceptive. Her mother had a pulmonary embolism. Coagulation testing shows resistance to activated protein C, and a point mutation in the factor V gene is found. How does this mutation promote thrombosis?
o: Factor Va cannot be inactivated by activated protein C
Factor V acts as an inhibitor of antithrombin
Factor V increases platelet adhesion to collagen
Factor V blocks the activation of plasminogen
questions.e: In factor V Leiden, a single amino-acid change removes the cleavage site for activated protein C, so factor Va persists and continues to generate thrombin. Oestrogen-containing contraception adds a further prothrombotic stimulus; the mutation does not affect antithrombin, platelets or fibrinolysis.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man receives an intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin at a clinic in Hyderabad. Within ten minutes he develops wheeze, generalised urticaria and a blood pressure of 70/40 mmHg. Which antibody mediates this reaction?
questions.e: Anaphylaxis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction: allergen cross-links specific IgE on mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and other mediators within minutes. IgG and IgM mediate type II and type III reactions, which take longer to develop.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, a diffuse goitre with a bruit and exophthalmos. Her TSH is suppressed and free T4 is raised. Which type of hypersensitivity underlies this disease?
questions.e: Graves disease is type II hypersensitivity: IgG antibodies bind a cell-surface antigen, the TSH receptor, and stimulate it, causing hyperthyroidism. Type III reactions involve circulating immune complexes deposited in vessels and glomeruli, not antibodies acting on a cell receptor.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy passes cola-coloured urine two weeks after a sore throat. His blood pressure is 130/90 mmHg and serum C3 is low. What would immunofluorescence of a renal biopsy most likely show?
o: Linear IgG along the glomerular basement membrane
Granular IgG and C3 along capillary walls
Dominant IgA deposits in the mesangium
questions.e: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is an immune-complex (type III) disease; deposited complexes give a lumpy-bumpy granular pattern of IgG and C3, and complement consumption lowers C3. Linear IgG is seen in anti-GBM disease, and mesangial IgA deposits occur in IgA nephropathy, which presents within days of an infection.

questions.s: A Mantoux test on a 30-year-old nurse in Karachi shows 15 mm of induration at 72 hours. Which cells are mainly responsible for this reaction?
questions.e: The tuberculin reaction is type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity: sensitised CD4+ Th1 cells recognise the antigen and release interferon-gamma, recruiting and activating macrophages over 48-72 hours. Mast cells and IgE produce immediate reactions within minutes.

questions.s: During a kidney transplant, the graft turns blue and mottled within minutes of the vascular clamps being released, and it must be removed. Histology shows widespread thrombosis of glomerular capillaries. What is the mechanism?
o: Donor T cells attacking recipient tissue
Preformed recipient antibodies against donor endothelium
Recipient CD8+ T cells killing donor tubular cells
Intimal fibrosis from chronic alloantibody injury
questions.e: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes when the recipient already has antibodies (for example ABO or anti-HLA) that bind donor endothelium, activate complement and cause thrombosis. CD8+ T-cell attack causes acute cellular rejection, which takes days to weeks, and donor T cells attacking the host is graft-versus-host disease.

questions.s: A 9-month-old boy has had three episodes of otitis media and two of pneumonia since the age of six months. His tonsils are barely visible. Serum IgG, IgA and IgM are all very low and flow cytometry shows almost no CD19+ cells. Which gene is most likely mutated?
o: Common gamma chain of cytokine receptors
questions.e: X-linked agammaglobulinaemia results from mutations in Bruton tyrosine kinase, which blocks B-cell maturation, so mature B cells and all immunoglobulin classes are absent; infections begin when maternal IgG wanes after about six months. CD40 ligand defects cause hyper-IgM syndrome, in which B cells are present and IgM is normal or high.

questions.s: A newborn has a seizure on day two with serum calcium of 6.2 mg/dL. Echocardiography shows truncus arteriosus, and a chest film shows no thymic shadow. Deficiency of which cell population will make him prone to viral and fungal infections?
questions.e: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) causes failure of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, with absent parathyroids (hypocalcaemia), conotruncal heart defects and thymic hypoplasia, leading to T-cell deficiency. B cells are present, although antibody responses can be reduced from lack of T-cell help.

questions.s: A 19-year-old man is admitted with his second episode of meningococcal meningitis in three years. He is otherwise well, with normal immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets. Deficiency of which complement component is most likely?
questions.e: The membrane attack complex (C5-C9) is particularly important in killing Neisseria, so deficiency of a terminal component predisposes to recurrent neisserial infection. Deficiencies of early classical components such as C1q and C4 are associated mainly with lupus-like disease, and C1 inhibitor deficiency causes hereditary angioedema.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has had bronchiectasis with daily purulent sputum for ten years. He now has nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows amorphous glomerular deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red staining under polarised light. What is the precursor protein of the deposit?
questions.e: Long-standing chronic inflammation (bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis) keeps serum amyloid A, an acute-phase protein, high, and its fragments deposit as AA (reactive systemic) amyloid, commonly in the kidney. Light-chain (AL) amyloid is associated with plasma cell disorders such as myeloma.

questions.s: Which feature most reliably establishes that a tumour is malignant rather than benign?
questions.e: Metastasis is the single unequivocal mark of malignancy; benign tumours never metastasise. Rapid growth, large size and mitoses can all occur in benign tumours, for example a leiomyoma in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has an abnormal cervical smear. A cervical biopsy shows atypical cells with high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio occupying the full thickness of the squamous epithelium, with an intact basement membrane. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Full-thickness dysplasia without breach of the basement membrane is carcinoma in situ (high-grade CIN 3); it cannot metastasise until the basement membrane is breached. Low-grade dysplasia is limited to the lower third, and microinvasive carcinoma shows small nests beyond the basement membrane.

questions.s: A 10-month-old girl has white pupillary reflexes in both eyes and is found to have bilateral retinoblastoma. Her father had an eye removed for the same tumour in infancy. Which mechanism best explains her tumours?
o: Activation of an oncogene by chromosomal translocation
Amplification of a growth factor receptor gene
Inherited mutant RB allele followed by a somatic hit
Defective DNA mismatch repair causing microsatellite instability
questions.e: Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: in familial retinoblastoma one RB allele is mutated in every cell from birth, so a single somatic mutation in a retinal cell is enough, giving early, bilateral tumours. RB is a tumour suppressor gene, so loss of both copies, not activation, is required.

questions.s: A 46-year-old woman has invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, and the tumour shows amplification of the HER2 (ERBB2) gene. She is offered treatment with a monoclonal antibody against its product. What kind of protein does HER2 encode?
questions.e: HER2 is a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase; amplification produces excess receptor and constant growth signals, and the antibody targets its extracellular domain. MYC is an example of an oncogenic transcription factor, and BCL2 an anti-apoptotic protein.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man who smokes heavily has a central hilar lung mass. Serum calcium is 13.2 mg/dL (8.5-10.5), parathyroid hormone is suppressed and an isotope bone scan shows no metastases. Bronchoscopic biopsy shows keratinising squamous cell carcinoma. Which tumour product most likely causes the hypercalcaemia?
questions.e: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung commonly secretes PTH-related peptide, which acts on PTH receptors to cause humoral hypercalcaemia while true PTH is suppressed. ACTH and ADH secretion are typical of small cell carcinoma, and calcitonin lowers rather than raises calcium.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C has a new 4 cm mass in the right lobe of the liver on ultrasound. Which serum tumour marker is most useful to support the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Hepatocellular carcinoma arises mainly in cirrhotic livers, especially with hepatitis B and C, and a raised alpha-fetoprotein supports the diagnosis. CA 19-9 is associated with pancreatic and biliary cancers, and CEA mainly with colorectal cancer.

questions.s: A 9-year-old boy has a rapidly enlarging mass in the right iliac fossa over three weeks. Biopsy shows sheets of uniform medium-sized lymphoid cells with scattered pale tingible-body macrophages giving a starry-sky pattern, and a proliferation index close to 100 %. Which chromosomal translocation is most characteristic?
questions.e: Burkitt lymphoma is driven by MYC on chromosome 8 translocated next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus on chromosome 14, causing extremely rapid proliferation; the sporadic form often presents in the ileocaecal region. t(14;18) involves BCL2 in follicular lymphoma, and t(11;14) involves cyclin D1 in mantle cell lymphoma.

questions.s: In a rural district, maize and groundnuts are stored for months in damp, poorly ventilated rooms and become contaminated with Aspergillus flavus. A toxin from this mould increases the risk of which cancer?
o: Squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
questions.e: Aflatoxin B1 from Aspergillus flavus is metabolised in the liver to a mutagen that causes a characteristic TP53 mutation, and it acts together with hepatitis B to cause hepatocellular carcinoma. Bladder cancer is linked with aromatic amines, smoking and schistosomiasis rather than aflatoxin.

questions.s: Normal human fibroblasts in culture stop dividing after about 60 population doublings, whereas cells from a carcinoma continue to divide indefinitely. Reactivation of which enzyme most often allows cancer cells to escape this limit?
questions.e: Each division shortens telomeres until a critical length triggers senescence; most cancers re-express telomerase, which adds telomeric repeats and confers limitless replicative potential. Topoisomerase II relieves DNA supercoiling during replication and is a target of some anticancer drugs, but it does not maintain telomeres.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman delivers a baby with a flat facial profile, upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease and an atrioventricular septal defect. The karyotype is 47,XX,+21. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Robertsonian translocation inherited from a parent
Mitotic error after fertilisation causing mosaicism
questions.e: About 95 % of Down syndrome is free trisomy 21, almost always from meiotic nondisjunction in the ovum, and the risk rises sharply with maternal age. A Robertsonian translocation would show 46 chromosomes with the extra 21 attached to another chromosome, and mosaicism would show a mixed cell population.

questions.s: A couple who are first cousins in Bahawalpur both have beta-thalassaemia trait. What is the chance that each pregnancy will result in a child with beta-thalassaemia major?
questions.e: Beta-thalassaemia major is autosomal recessive; when both parents are carriers, each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child, a 1 in 2 chance of a carrier and a 1 in 4 chance of an unaffected non-carrier. Consanguineous marriage raises the chance that both partners carry the same mutation.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy has moderate intellectual disability, a long face with large prominent ears, a prominent jaw and enlarged testes. His maternal uncle is similarly affected. Which genetic mechanism is most likely?
o: CTG repeat expansion in the DMPK gene
CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene
questions.e: Fragile X syndrome is caused by an expanded CGG trinucleotide repeat in FMR1 on the X chromosome, which silences the gene; macro-orchidism, long face and large ears are typical, and the expansion grows through female carriers. CTG expansion in DMPK causes myotonic dystrophy.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl was very floppy and fed poorly as a newborn, but now has an insatiable appetite, obesity, small hands and feet and developmental delay. Methylation studies of chromosome 15q11-q13 are abnormal. What is the most common underlying mechanism of her condition?
o: Deletion on the paternally derived chromosome 15
Deletion on the maternally derived chromosome 15
questions.e: Prader-Willi syndrome results from loss of the paternally expressed genes at 15q11-q13, most often a deletion on the paternal chromosome (maternal uniparental disomy is the next commonest cause), because the maternal copies are imprinted and silent. A deletion on the maternal chromosome, or paternal uniparental disomy, causes Angelman syndrome.

questions.s: A woman's brother has haemophilia A, and genetic testing confirms that she is a carrier. Her husband is healthy. What is the chance that any son she has will be affected?
questions.e: Haemophilia A is X-linked recessive; a carrier mother passes her affected X to half of her sons, who will have the disease, and to half of her daughters, who will be carriers. The 25 % figure is the risk for any child of unknown sex, not specifically for a son.

questions.s: In a family with an inherited optic neuropathy, every child of affected women inherits the disorder, though severity varies widely, while no child of an affected man is ever affected. Which mode of inheritance fits best?
questions.e: Mitochondria are inherited only from the ovum, so mitochondrial DNA disorders pass from mothers to all their children and never from fathers; variable severity reflects heteroplasmy. In X-linked dominant inheritance an affected father passes the disorder to all his daughters, which is not seen here.

questions.s: A 15-year-old girl has not started menstruating. She is short, with a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples and a higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs. Which karyotype is most likely?
questions.e: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes short stature, webbed neck, primary amenorrhoea from streak ovaries, and coarctation of the aorta, which explains the arm-leg blood pressure difference. 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome in a phenotypic male.

questions.s: Within minutes of a fall in ATP in hypoxic renal tubular cells, the plasma membrane sodium pump fails. Which light-microscopic change does this produce first?
questions.e: Failure of the Na+/K+-ATPase lets sodium and water enter the cell, causing cellular (hydropic) swelling, the earliest and reversible change visible by light microscopy. Karyorrhexis is nuclear fragmentation, a feature of established cell death.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has had his left leg in a plaster cast for eight weeks after a tibial fracture. On removal, the left calf is clearly thinner than the right. Which process explains this?
questions.e: Atrophy is a reduction in the size of cells and of an organ that was once normal, here from disuse of the immobilised muscle. Hypoplasia and aplasia describe incomplete or absent development of an organ, not shrinkage of an established one.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has a big toe that is black, dry, shrivelled and cold, with a sharp line of demarcation from healthy skin. There is no swelling or discharge. What is this?
questions.e: Dry gangrene follows slow arterial occlusion: the tissue undergoes coagulative necrosis, dries and mummifies, with a clear line of demarcation. Wet gangrene results from superimposed bacterial infection with liquefaction, swelling and foul discharge.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man who drinks heavily has an enlarged, yellow, greasy liver. Biopsy shows hepatocytes containing large clear vacuoles that push the nucleus to the side. What has accumulated in these cells?
questions.e: Alcohol increases fatty acid synthesis and reduces their oxidation, so triglycerides accumulate as macrovesicular fat droplets that displace the nucleus (steatosis), a reversible change if drinking stops. Glycogen accumulation gives pale cytoplasm without a single large vacuole.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man has primary angioplasty that restores flow in an occluded coronary artery four hours after symptom onset. Some myocytes that were still viable before reperfusion now die. What is the main mechanism of this additional damage?
questions.e: Reperfusion injury occurs when oxygen returns to damaged cells whose antioxidant defences are impaired, producing reactive oxygen species, along with calcium overload and an inflammatory influx. It is not caused by continuing ischaemia, since flow has been restored.

questions.s: In the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis, which event leads directly to activation of caspase-9 through formation of the apoptosome?
o: Granzyme B entry through perforin pores
questions.e: When BAX and BAK permeabilise the outer mitochondrial membrane, cytochrome c enters the cytosol, binds APAF-1 and forms the apoptosome, which activates caspase-9. Fas ligand and TNF act through death receptors and caspase-8 in the extrinsic pathway.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism has a serum calcium of 12.8 mg/dL (8.5-10.5). Autopsy after an unrelated death shows calcium deposits in the gastric mucosa, renal interstitium and alveolar walls, all of which were otherwise healthy. What type of calcification is this?
questions.e: Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues when serum calcium is high, and favours tissues that lose acid (gastric mucosa, kidney, lungs), where the local alkaline environment promotes deposition. Dystrophic calcification occurs in damaged tissue despite normal serum calcium.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has had recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, a liver abscess and pneumonia caused by Aspergillus. A dihydrorhodamine flow cytometry test shows no oxidative burst in his neutrophils. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.e: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by defective NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes cannot generate the respiratory burst needed to kill catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus. Myeloperoxidase deficiency is common and usually mild because hydrogen peroxide is still produced.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy has silvery hair, light skin, recurrent pyogenic infections and nystagmus. A blood film shows giant cytoplasmic granules in neutrophils. Which protein is defective?
questions.e: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutations in LYST, which disturbs fusion of lysosomes with phagosomes, producing giant granules, poor bacterial killing and partial albinism from abnormal melanosomes. NADPH oxidase defects cause chronic granulomatous disease without albinism or giant granules.

questions.s: Which chemical mediator, generated from kininogen, is a major cause of pain in acute inflammation?
questions.e: Bradykinin, produced from high-molecular-weight kininogen by kallikrein, increases vascular permeability and stimulates pain receptors, an effect enhanced by prostaglandins. Leukotriene B4 and IL-8 act mainly as neutrophil chemoattractants.

questions.s: In the recruitment of neutrophils to a site of infection, the first step is loose, transient attachment that makes the cells roll along the venular endothelium. Which molecules mediate rolling?
questions.e: Rolling is mediated by selectins (E- and P-selectin on endothelium, L-selectin on leukocytes) binding sialylated carbohydrate ligands with low affinity. Integrins binding ICAM-1 mediate the next step of firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 mediates transmigration.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has a firm nodule in her caesarean section scar from two years ago. Excision shows a collection of macrophages and multinucleate giant cells surrounding fragments of refractile, polarisable material, without caseation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Giant cells clustered around inert polarisable material such as suture fragments form a foreign body granuloma. A tuberculous granuloma shows caseous necrosis with Langhans giant cells and no foreign material.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis has an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 85 mm in the first hour. A rise in which plasma protein mainly causes red cells to form rouleaux and sediment faster?
questions.e: Fibrinogen is an acute-phase protein that neutralises the negative surface charge of red cells, so they stack into rouleaux and sediment faster, raising the ESR. Albumin falls in inflammation and, if anything, slows sedimentation.

questions.s: A 10-year-old girl from a village in southern Punjab, who walks barefoot, has iron deficiency anaemia. Her white cell count is 11 x 10^9/L with 22 % eosinophils. What is the most likely cause of the eosinophilia?
questions.e: Eosinophilia is typical of tissue-invasive helminth infection; walking barefoot and iron deficiency suggest hookworm, whose larvae penetrate skin and whose adults cause intestinal blood loss. Bacterial infections cause neutrophilia, and typhoid characteristically causes leucopenia with absent eosinophils.

questions.s: A skin wound is examined histologically at five days. Which type of collagen is mainly deposited in the early granulation tissue before being replaced in the maturing scar?
questions.e: Early granulation tissue is rich in type III collagen, which is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen as the scar remodels. Type II collagen is found in cartilage, and type IV in basement membranes.

questions.s: In a healing skin wound, new capillaries sprout from existing vessels to form granulation tissue. Which growth factor is the main stimulus for this angiogenesis?
questions.e: VEGF, released by macrophages and hypoxic cells, stimulates endothelial migration, proliferation and increased permeability, driving new vessel formation in granulation tissue. EGF acts mainly on keratinocytes, stimulating re-epithelialisation.

questions.s: A clean surgical incision closed with sutures is examined histologically 24 hours after the operation. Which finding is expected at this stage?
o: Neutrophils at the margins and a fibrin clot
questions.e: In healing by first intention, the incision fills with blood clot and fibrin within hours, and by 24 hours neutrophils appear at the wound margins while the epidermis begins to thicken. Granulation tissue peaks around day 5, collagen bridges the gap by about the second week, and a pale scar forms later.

questions.s: An 18-year-old boy has a closed fracture of the tibial shaft treated in a cast. Which tissue mainly forms the soft callus that bridges the fracture ends at about two to three weeks?
questions.e: After the haematoma is organised, osteoprogenitor cells and chondroblasts form a soft callus of fibrocartilage and woven bone that bridges the fracture; this is later replaced by bony callus and remodelled into lamellar bone over months. A purely fibrous union indicates failure of normal healing.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C has progressive liver fibrosis on serial biopsies. Which cell, activated by TGF-beta, is the main source of the collagen deposited in the liver?
questions.e: Hepatic stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse normally store vitamin A, but when activated by TGF-beta and other cytokines they become myofibroblast-like and lay down collagen, causing fibrosis and cirrhosis. Kupffer cells release cytokines that activate stellate cells but do not produce most of the collagen.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has a leg wound healing by secondary intention. After three weeks, a soft red mass of tissue protrudes above the level of the surrounding skin and prevents the epithelium from covering the wound. What is this called?
questions.e: Excess granulation tissue that rises above the skin surface (proud flesh) blocks re-epithelialisation and may need cautery or excision. Keloid and hypertrophic scar are firm collagen-rich scars that form after epithelial cover, not soft vascular tissue.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, who is not on anticoagulation, suddenly develops right-sided weakness and loss of speech. Where did the embolus most likely originate?
questions.e: In atrial fibrillation, stasis in the poorly contracting left atrium, especially the appendage, allows thrombus to form and embolise to the systemic arteries, most often the brain. Leg vein thrombi travel to the lungs unless there is a right-to-left shunt.

questions.s: A deep vein thrombus is examined several weeks after it formed. It is firmly attached to the vein wall and has been invaded by endothelial cells, smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts, with new channels that restore some flow. What process is this?
questions.e: Older thrombi are organised by ingrowth of cells and capillaries, and new vascular channels may re-establish some flow (recanalisation). Fibrinolysis can dissolve only recent thrombi, before extensive fibrin cross-linking and organisation have occurred.

questions.s: A 34-year-old diver ascends rapidly from a depth of 30 m. Within an hour he has severe pain in the knees and shoulders and tightness in the chest. Bubbles of which gas cause this condition?
questions.e: At depth, extra nitrogen dissolves in blood and tissues; rapid decompression lets it come out of solution as bubbles in joints, lungs and vessels, causing decompression sickness (the bends). Oxygen is used up by tissues and does not form persistent bubbles.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman in active labour suddenly becomes breathless and hypotensive, has a seizure, and then bleeds from cannula sites. She dies despite resuscitation. Which autopsy finding would confirm the diagnosis?
o: Fetal squames in maternal pulmonary vessels
Laminated thrombus in the leg veins
questions.e: Amniotic fluid embolism causes sudden respiratory distress, shock, seizures and DIC during labour; autopsy shows fetal squamous cells, lanugo hair and mucin in the maternal pulmonary microcirculation. Pulmonary thromboembolism does not cause early DIC and seizures in this way.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has lost about 2 litres of blood after a road traffic accident. His blood pressure is 80/50 mmHg and serum lactate is 6 mmol/L (normal below 2). What is the main reason for the raised lactate?
o: Loss of bicarbonate in the urine
questions.e: Poor tissue perfusion in shock forces cells to rely on anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid; a rising lactate indicates inadequate resuscitation. Haemoglobin itself carries oxygen normally here; the problem is reduced delivery from low flow.

questions.s: During vigorous exercise, the blood flow to skeletal muscle increases greatly as arterioles dilate. What is this increase in blood volume in a tissue called?
questions.e: Active hyperaemia is an increased inflow of blood from arteriolar dilation, which makes tissue red and warm, as in exercise or inflammation. Passive congestion results from impaired venous outflow and gives a dusky, cyanotic colour.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man survives a cardiac arrest with prolonged hypotension but dies a week later. Autopsy shows wedge-shaped cortical infarcts in a strip where the territories of the anterior and middle cerebral arteries meet. What is the mechanism?
o: Embolism to the middle cerebral artery
Hypoperfusion of the border zones between arterial territories
Thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus
questions.e: Watershed (border zone) infarcts occur in areas at the farthest reaches of two arterial supplies, which are the first to suffer when systemic pressure falls. An embolus would produce an infarct within a single arterial territory.

questions.s: A 30-year-old farmer from Tharparkar receives polyvalent anti-snake venom after a viper bite. Ten days later he develops fever, urticaria, joint pains and proteinuria, with low serum complement. What is the mechanism?
questions.e: Serum sickness is a type III hypersensitivity reaction: antibodies form against the foreign animal proteins in antivenom, and the resulting immune complexes deposit in vessels, joints and glomeruli, consuming complement. Immediate IgE-mediated reactions to antivenom occur within minutes, not after 1-2 weeks.

questions.s: During a blood transfusion, a 45-year-old woman develops fever, loin pain and dark red urine within 15 minutes. It is found that she received a unit meant for another patient. What is the mechanism of red cell destruction?
o: Complement-fixing IgM against donor red cells
questions.e: In an ABO-incompatible transfusion, the recipient's naturally occurring anti-A or anti-B IgM binds donor red cells and activates complement, causing intravascular haemolysis and haemoglobinuria, a type II hypersensitivity. Immune complex disease takes days to develop.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man receives an allogeneic bone marrow transplant for aplastic anaemia. Three weeks later he has a widespread rash, profuse diarrhoea and jaundice. Which cells cause this complication?
o: Donor T lymphocytes reacting to host antigens
questions.e: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T cells recognise the host's tissues as foreign, targeting skin, gut and bile ducts. Rejection of the graft by the recipient's own immune system is the reverse process and would cause marrow failure instead.

questions.s: A 4-month-old girl has persistent oral thrush, chronic diarrhoea and failure to thrive, and now has Pneumocystis pneumonia. Her lymphocyte count is very low and no thymic shadow is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe combined immunodeficiency affects both T-cell and B-cell function, so opportunistic infections such as candida and Pneumocystis appear in the first months of life, with lymphopenia and a small thymus. X-linked agammaglobulinaemia affects only B cells, mainly causes bacterial infections and occurs in boys.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman has a history of recurrent sinusitis and giardiasis. During her first blood transfusion after childbirth, she develops severe anaphylaxis. What underlying condition is most likely?
questions.e: Selective IgA deficiency is the commonest primary antibody deficiency; patients may have sinopulmonary and giardia infections, and some form anti-IgA antibodies that cause anaphylaxis when given blood products containing IgA. C1 inhibitor deficiency causes recurrent angioedema without urticaria, not transfusion anaphylaxis.

questions.s: A 24-year-old woman has a malar rash, painful joints, mouth ulcers and proteinuria of 2 g per day. Which autoantibody is most specific for her disease and correlates best with renal involvement?
questions.e: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for systemic lupus erythematosus, and their titre tends to follow disease activity, especially lupus nephritis. ANA is very sensitive but not specific, and anti-histone antibodies suggest drug-induced lupus.

questions.s: A liver cell infected with hepatitis B virus is killed by a cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocyte. On which molecules does the infected cell present the viral peptide to this T cell?
questions.e: Almost all nucleated cells present peptides from intracellular proteins, including viral proteins, on MHC class I, which is recognised by CD8+ T cells. MHC class II is found mainly on antigen-presenting cells and presents to CD4+ helper T cells.

questions.s: A 42-year-old woman has heavy menstrual bleeding. Ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus with several well-circumscribed masses. Hysterectomy shows firm, grey-white, whorled nodules composed of bland smooth muscle cells. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Leiomyomas (fibroids) are benign smooth muscle tumours: well circumscribed, whorled on cut section and made of uniform cells with few mitoses. Leiomyosarcoma shows necrosis, nuclear atypia and many mitoses, and is usually a single, soft, fleshy mass.

questions.s: Carcinomas usually spread first to regional lymph nodes. Which carcinoma characteristically spreads by the bloodstream, often invading the renal vein and inferior vena cava?
o: Squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
questions.e: Renal cell carcinoma tends to invade the renal vein, sometimes growing as a tumour column into the inferior vena cava, and metastasises by blood to lungs and bone. Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the classic example of a carcinoma that spreads to lymph nodes.

questions.s: After exposure to ionising radiation, a normal cell with DNA damage halts in the G1 phase of the cell cycle until repair is done. Which p53-induced protein directly inhibits the cyclin-dependent kinases to cause this arrest?
questions.e: p53 transcriptionally activates the CDK inhibitor p21, which blocks cyclin-CDK complexes so that RB stays unphosphorylated and the cell cannot enter S phase. MDM2 is also induced by p53, but it degrades p53 as negative feedback rather than inhibiting CDKs.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix positive for HPV type 16. The viral E7 protein contributes to carcinogenesis by binding and inactivating which host protein?
questions.e: HPV E7 binds the hypophosphorylated RB protein, releasing E2F transcription factors and pushing cells through the G1/S checkpoint. The E6 protein, not E7, promotes degradation of p53.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with advanced pancreatic carcinoma has lost 15 kg despite reasonable food intake, with marked loss of muscle and fat. Which mediator released by host macrophages contributes most to this cachexia?
questions.e: Cancer cachexia is driven by cytokines such as TNF (and IL-6) together with tumour-derived factors, which suppress appetite, mobilise fat and break down muscle protein. It is not explained by reduced intake alone; insulin is anabolic and would oppose these changes.

questions.s: A 1 cm submucosal nodule is removed from the wall of the gastric antrum of a 35-year-old woman. Histology shows normal pancreatic acini and ducts with no atypia. What is the correct term for this lesion?
questions.e: A choristoma (heterotopic rest) is normal tissue in an abnormal location, such as pancreatic tissue in the stomach wall. A hamartoma is a disorganised overgrowth of tissue native to that site, such as a lung hamartoma containing cartilage and bronchial epithelium.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man attends an infertility clinic. He is tall with long legs, has bilateral gynaecomastia and small firm testes. Semen analysis shows no sperm and FSH is markedly raised. What is the most likely karyotype?
questions.e: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes testicular atrophy with azoospermia, high gonadotrophins from lack of feedback, tall stature and gynaecomastia. 47,XYY men are tall but usually have normal testes and fertility.

questions.s: A tall 20-year-old man has long fingers, a high-arched palate, upward dislocation of both lenses and a dilated aortic root on echocardiography. His father died suddenly of aortic dissection. A defect in which protein is most likely?
questions.e: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant defect of fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein scaffold for elastic fibres, affecting the skeleton, the suspensory ligament of the lens and the aortic media. Type III collagen defects cause vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, with arterial rupture but without lens dislocation.

questions.s: An 8-year-old girl has massive splenomegaly, bone pain and pancytopenia. A bone marrow aspirate shows large macrophages whose cytoplasm looks like crumpled tissue paper. Deficiency of which enzyme is most likely?
questions.e: Gaucher disease, the commonest lysosomal storage disorder, results from glucocerebrosidase deficiency; glucocerebroside accumulates in macrophages, giving characteristic Gaucher cells, hepatosplenomegaly and bone disease. Sphingomyelinase deficiency (Niemann-Pick disease) produces foamy, vacuolated macrophages.

questions.s: A 5-year-old boy has difficulty climbing stairs, uses his hands to push himself up from the floor and has enlarged calves. Creatine kinase is 15,000 U/L. Which type of mutation in the dystrophin gene is found most often in this disorder?
o: A deletion that shifts the reading frame
questions.e: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is most often caused by large deletions in the very large dystrophin gene that disrupt the reading frame, so no functional protein is made. In-frame deletions allow a shortened, partly working dystrophin and cause the milder Becker dystrophy.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman has her second child with Down syndrome. The child's karyotype has 46 chromosomes, with the extra chromosome 21 joined to a chromosome 14. What is the most appropriate next step for the family?
questions.e: Translocation Down syndrome may arise from a parent carrying a balanced Robertsonian translocation, which carries a high recurrence risk, so both parents should be karyotyped for counselling. In free trisomy 21 the recurrence risk is low and related mainly to maternal age.

questions.s: A 12-year-old girl from Swat has fever, migrating pain in the knees and ankles and a new apical pansystolic murmur three weeks after a sore throat. ASO titre is raised. If myocardium were examined histologically, which lesion would be characteristic?
o: Caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells
questions.e: Acute rheumatic fever produces a pancarditis with Aschoff bodies, foci of fibrinoid change surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells and Anitschkow cells with caterpillar-like nuclei. Asteroid bodies in non-caseating granulomas suggest sarcoidosis, not rheumatic carditis.

questions.s: At the autopsy of an 18-year-old man killed in a road accident, flat yellow streaks are seen on the inner surface of the thoracic aorta, not raised enough to disturb flow. Which cells mainly form these streaks?
questions.e: Fatty streaks, the earliest lesions of atherosclerosis, consist of intimal foam cells, mainly macrophages that have taken up oxidised LDL; they can be present in adolescence. Calcification appears later in complicated atheromatous plaques.

questions.s: A 38-year-old man who has never smoked has progressive breathlessness. CT shows emphysema mainly in the lower lobes, and he has mildly deranged liver function tests. Deficiency of which protein is most likely?
questions.e: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency allows neutrophil elastase to destroy alveolar walls unopposed, giving early panacinar emphysema with lower-lobe predominance, and the misfolded protein accumulates in hepatocytes causing liver disease. Smoking-related emphysema is centriacinar and affects the upper lobes.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has generalised oedema, heavy selective proteinuria and normal blood pressure, with no haematuria. He responds completely to oral prednisolone. If a renal biopsy had been taken, what would electron microscopy have shown?
o: Diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes
Splitting and lamination of the basement membrane
questions.e: Minimal change disease, the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children, shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy and only diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy, with excellent response to steroids. Subepithelial humps are seen in post-infectious glomerulonephritis.

questions.s: A 48-year-old man who drinks heavily has jaundice, fever and tender hepatomegaly, with AST more than twice ALT. Liver biopsy shows ballooned hepatocytes containing clumped eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions, with a neutrophil infiltrate. What are these inclusions?
questions.e: Mallory-Denk bodies are tangled cytokeratin intermediate filaments in injured hepatocytes, typical of alcoholic hepatitis together with ballooning and neutrophils. Ground-glass hepatocytes contain hepatitis B surface antigen, and Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes in viral hepatitis.

questions.s: A 9-year-old girl in Lahore has chronic diarrhoea, abdominal distension, short stature and iron deficiency that does not respond to oral iron. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA is strongly positive. What would a duodenal biopsy most likely show?
o: Villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and many intraepithelial lymphocytes
Foamy PAS-positive macrophages in the lamina propria
questions.e: Coeliac disease is gluten-sensitive enteropathy: the duodenal mucosa shows villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes, and iron is malabsorbed in the proximal bowel. PAS-positive macrophages are typical of Whipple disease.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has an ileocolic resection for a stricture causing obstruction. The specimen shows segments of diseased bowel separated by normal bowel, transmural inflammation, deep fissures and small non-caseating granulomas. Acid-fast stains are negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Skip lesions, transmural inflammation, fissuring ulcers and non-caseating granulomas are characteristic of Crohn disease. Intestinal tuberculosis, an important differential in Pakistan, typically shows large confluent caseating granulomas, and ulcerative colitis is continuous and limited to the mucosa of the colon.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman has tiredness, weight gain and a firm, painless, diffusely enlarged thyroid. TSH is raised and anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies are strongly positive. What would thyroid histology most likely show?
o: Papillae lined by cells with optically clear nuclei
Tall hyperplastic follicles with scalloped colloid
questions.e: Hashimoto thyroiditis is autoimmune destruction of the gland: a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate with germinal centres, atrophic follicles and oxyphil (Hurthle) cells. Granulomas with giant cells suggest subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, and scalloped colloid with hyperplastic follicles is seen in Graves disease.

questions.s: A 58-year-old woman has had type 2 diabetes for 20 years and now has proteinuria of 3 g per day. Renal biopsy shows rounded PAS-positive nodules of mesangial matrix at the periphery of glomeruli; Congo red stain is negative. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules of PAS-positive mesangial matrix are specific for diabetic nephropathy, which follows years of diabetes along with basement membrane thickening and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. Amyloid can also form nodules but stains with Congo red.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman who has never smoked has a 3 cm peripheral mass in the right upper lobe. Biopsy shows a gland-forming tumour producing mucin, positive for TTF-1, and an activating EGFR mutation is found. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Adenocarcinoma is the commonest lung cancer in never-smokers and women; it is usually peripheral, forms glands, expresses TTF-1, and EGFR mutations are particularly frequent in this group. Squamous and small cell carcinomas are strongly linked to smoking and are typically central.

questions.s: A 15-year-old boy has had increasing pain around the left knee for two months. X-ray shows a destructive lesion in the metaphysis of the distal femur, with a sunburst periosteal pattern and a Codman triangle. Biopsy shows pleomorphic malignant cells laying down osteoid. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Osteosarcoma occurs in adolescents around the knee, in the metaphysis, and the diagnostic feature is malignant cells producing osteoid. Ewing sarcoma usually arises in the diaphysis and consists of small round blue cells without osteoid.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has had headaches for six weeks and a first seizure. MRI shows a ring-enhancing mass crossing the corpus callosum. Histology shows pleomorphic astrocytic cells, areas of necrosis surrounded by palisading tumour cells and glomeruloid vascular proliferation. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Necrosis with pseudopalisading and microvascular proliferation define glioblastoma, the commonest primary malignant brain tumour in adults, which often spreads across the corpus callosum (butterfly glioma). Metastases are usually multiple at the grey-white junction and consist of epithelial cells, not astrocytic cells.

questions.s: A 32-year-old man has a painless, firm swelling of the right testis. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is normal. Orchidectomy shows sheets of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm and central nuclei, separated by fibrous septa containing lymphocytes. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Seminoma is the commonest testicular germ cell tumour, made of sheets of clear cells divided by septa with lymphocytes, and it does not produce alpha-fetoprotein. Yolk sac tumour shows Schiller-Duval bodies and secretes AFP, and is commonest in young children.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has an ill-defined thickening in the left breast. Biopsy shows small, uniform, non-cohesive tumour cells infiltrating the stroma in single-file strands, and immunohistochemistry shows loss of E-cadherin. What is the diagnosis?
o: Invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type
questions.e: Invasive lobular carcinoma typically grows as single files of small discohesive cells because the adhesion molecule E-cadherin is lost; it is more often bilateral or multicentric. Invasive ductal carcinoma usually forms cohesive nests and glands and retains E-cadherin.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has menorrhagia and tiredness. Haemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL (80-100), and serum ferritin is 6 ng/mL (15-150). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Microcytic anaemia with a very low ferritin is diagnostic of iron deficiency, here from menstrual blood loss. Beta-thalassaemia trait also causes microcytosis, but the ferritin is normal and haemoglobin is usually only mildly reduced.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has premarital screening in Karachi. His haemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL, MCV 63 fL, red cell count 6.2 x 10^12/L and serum ferritin is normal. Which investigation will best confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Marked microcytosis with a high red cell count, near-normal haemoglobin and normal ferritin suggests beta-thalassaemia trait, which is confirmed by a raised HbA2 (above 3.5 %) on HPLC or electrophoresis. Identifying carriers before marriage allows counselling of couples about the risk of thalassaemia major.

questions.s: A 60-year-old woman has tiredness, tingling in the feet and loss of vibration and joint position sense in the legs. Haemoglobin is 8.6 g/dL, MCV 118 fL, and the film shows hypersegmented neutrophils. What is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Megaloblastic anaemia with dorsal column signs points to vitamin B12 deficiency, and in this age group the commonest cause is pernicious anaemia, in which autoantibodies to intrinsic factor and parietal cells prevent B12 absorption. Folate deficiency causes a similar anaemia but not subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

questions.s: A 10-year-old boy has had several episodes of jaundice and has an enlarged spleen. His father had a splenectomy as a young man. The blood film shows many small dense round red cells without central pallor, the MCHC is raised and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. What is the underlying defect?
questions.e: Hereditary spherocytosis, usually autosomal dominant, results from defects in membrane skeleton proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin or band 3; the cells lose membrane, become spherical and are destroyed in the spleen. A negative DAT distinguishes it from autoimmune haemolysis, which also produces spherocytes.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy is treated with primaquine for Plasmodium vivax malaria. Two days later he becomes pale and passes dark urine. The blood film shows red cells with bites taken out of them. Which inclusions would a supravital stain show in his red cells?
questions.e: In G6PD deficiency, oxidant drugs such as primaquine denature haemoglobin into Heinz bodies, which splenic macrophages remove, leaving bite cells. Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear remnants seen after splenectomy, and basophilic stippling suggests lead poisoning or thalassaemia.

questions.s: A 1-year-old boy from rural Sindh has had increasing pallor since the age of six months and has marked hepatosplenomegaly. Haemoglobin is 5.1 g/dL, MCV 58 fL and the film shows target cells and many nucleated red cells. His parents are first cousins. What would haemoglobin HPLC most likely show?
o: Very high HbF with little or no HbA
questions.e: In beta-thalassaemia major, beta-chain synthesis is absent or severely reduced, so HbA is absent or minimal and HbF is very high; symptoms begin as the switch from gamma to beta chains occurs at around six months. A raised HbA2 with normal HbA describes the carrier state.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has haemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, MCV 82 fL, low serum iron, low TIBC and serum ferritin of 320 ng/mL. Increased production of which hormone mainly causes her anaemia?
questions.e: In anaemia of chronic disease, IL-6 drives hepatic hepcidin production; hepcidin degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in macrophages and blocking intestinal absorption, so serum iron is low while ferritin is normal or high. Erythropoietin production is, if anything, inappropriately low in this condition.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has easy bruising, recurrent mouth infections and pallor. There is no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Haemoglobin is 6.8 g/dL, white cells 1.2 x 10^9/L, platelets 12 x 10^9/L and reticulocytes 0.2 %. What will a bone marrow trephine most likely show?
questions.e: Pancytopenia with a very low reticulocyte count and no organomegaly suggests aplastic anaemia, where the trephine shows markedly hypocellular marrow replaced by fat. A trephine is essential, because an aspirate from a hypocellular or fibrotic marrow may be a dry tap.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has abdominal fullness and early satiety. His spleen is palpable 15 cm below the costal margin. White cell count is 180 x 10^9/L with neutrophils, myelocytes, metamyelocytes and a few blasts, and absolute basophilia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Massive splenomegaly with a very high white count showing the full spectrum of myeloid maturation and basophilia is typical of chronic myeloid leukaemia, caused by the BCR-ABL1 fusion from t(9;22). A leukaemoid reaction has a clear cause, no basophilia and no massive splenomegaly.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has bleeding gums and widespread bruising. The blood film shows abnormal promyelocytes with bundles of Auer rods, platelets are 18 x 10^9/L and fibrinogen is 0.8 g/L (2-4). Which genetic abnormality is most likely?
questions.e: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia results from t(15;17), producing the PML-RARA fusion; the granular promyelocytes release procoagulants that cause DIC, and all-trans retinoic acid induces their maturation. t(8;21) and inv(16) define other acute myeloid leukaemias with a good prognosis but are not typically associated with DIC.

questions.s: A 4-year-old boy has bone pain, pallor, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly. Bone marrow shows 85 % blasts with scanty cytoplasm and no granules. Positivity for which marker in the blasts would best confirm a lymphoblastic leukaemia?
questions.e: TdT is a DNA polymerase expressed in the nuclei of immature lymphoid cells, so it is positive in lymphoblasts of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the commonest childhood cancer. Myeloperoxidase is a marker of myeloid blasts, and TRAP is characteristic of hairy cell leukaemia.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man has a routine blood count before cataract surgery. He feels well and has small painless cervical nodes. White cell count is 52 x 10^9/L, 90 % small mature lymphocytes with many smudge cells, and the cells are CD5 and CD23 positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is a disease of older adults with a lymphocytosis of small mature B cells co-expressing CD5 and CD23, and fragile cells that form smudge cells on the film. Infectious mononucleosis produces large reactive (atypical) lymphocytes in younger patients.

questions.s: A 22-year-old man has painless cervical lymphadenopathy, night sweats and itching. Node biopsy shows nodules separated by collagen bands, containing occasional large binucleate cells with prominent owl-eye nucleoli in a background of lymphocytes and eosinophils. Which markers do the large cells typically express?
questions.e: The large cells are Reed-Sternberg cells of classical Hodgkin lymphoma (here the nodular sclerosis type), which typically express CD15 and CD30 and lack CD45. CD20 with CD10 suggests a germinal-centre B-cell lymphoma, and CD34 with TdT marks lymphoblasts.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man has back pain and constipation. Serum calcium is 11.8 mg/dL, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, ESR 110 mm/hour, the blood film shows rouleaux and a skull X-ray shows punched-out lytic lesions. What would serum protein electrophoresis most likely show?
o: Isolated rise in the alpha-1 band
questions.e: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma cell neoplasm that produces a single immunoglobulin, seen as a narrow M band; with bone lesions, hypercalcaemia and renal impairment it fulfils the classic picture. A broad polyclonal rise is seen in chronic inflammation and liver disease.

questions.s: A 2-year-old boy has a hot, swollen right knee after a minor fall. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. Which pattern of results is expected?
o: Prolonged APTT, normal PT, normal platelet count
Prolonged PT, normal APTT, normal platelet count
Prolonged PT and APTT with a low platelet count
Normal PT and APTT with a low platelet count
questions.e: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency), X-linked recessive, affects the intrinsic pathway, so the APTT is prolonged while the PT and platelet count are normal; haemarthrosis is the typical bleed. A prolonged PT alone suggests factor VII deficiency, early vitamin K deficiency or warfarin.

questions.s: A 19-year-old woman has had heavy periods since menarche, frequent nosebleeds and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Her mother has similar problems. Platelet count is 260 x 10^9/L, PT is normal and APTT is slightly prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Von Willebrand disease, usually autosomal dominant, causes mucocutaneous bleeding in both sexes; the APTT may be mildly prolonged because von Willebrand factor carries and protects factor VIII. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is autosomal recessive and does not affect the APTT.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl develops petechiae and bruising two weeks after a viral illness. She is otherwise well with no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Platelets are 9 x 10^9/L with large platelets on the film; haemoglobin and white cells are normal. What is the mechanism of the thrombocytopenia?
o: IgG-coated platelets removed in the spleen
Pooling of platelets in an enlarged spleen
questions.e: Childhood immune thrombocytopenia follows viral infections: antibodies coat platelets, which are removed by splenic macrophages, while the marrow responds with increased megakaryocytes and large young platelets. Marrow failure would also affect red and white cells.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has fever, confusion and petechiae. Haemoglobin is 7.0 g/dL with many schistocytes on the film, platelets are 15 x 10^9/L, LDH is very high and creatinine is 1.6 mg/dL. PT and APTT are normal. Severe deficiency of which protein is most likely?
questions.e: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, usually from autoantibodies; ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers then form platelet microthrombi, producing microangiopathic haemolysis, thrombocytopenia and organ damage. Normal PT and APTT help distinguish it from DIC.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman is admitted to a THQ hospital with septicaemia after an unsafe abortion. She is oozing blood from cannula sites and the uterus. Which set of results is most likely?
o: Low platelets, long PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer
Low platelets, normal PT and APTT, normal fibrinogen, normal D-dimer
Normal platelets, long APTT only, normal fibrinogen, normal D-dimer
Normal platelets, long PT only, normal fibrinogen, high D-dimer
questions.e: Disseminated intravascular coagulation in sepsis consumes platelets and clotting factors, prolonging PT and APTT and lowering fibrinogen, while fibrinolysis of widespread microthrombi raises D-dimer. Isolated thrombocytopenia with normal clotting suggests immune thrombocytopenia instead.

questions.s: A 3-week-old boy born at home in a village and exclusively breastfed is brought with bleeding from the umbilicus and a bulging fontanelle. He did not receive any injection at birth. Platelets are normal and PT is markedly prolonged. Deficiency of which clotting factors explains this?
o: Factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.e: Vitamin K deficiency bleeding occurs in breastfed babies who miss prophylactic vitamin K, because breast milk is low in it and gut flora are not established; the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S) are reduced. Factors VIII and IX are deficient in the haemophilias, which do not prolong the PT.

questions.s: A 62-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is started on warfarin. His INR begins to rise within 1-2 days, although full anticoagulation takes several days. The early rise mainly reflects falling levels of which factor, which has the shortest half-life?
questions.e: Factor VII has a half-life of about 6 hours, so it falls first after warfarin and prolongs the PT/INR early, before prothrombin (half-life about 3 days) has fallen enough for full antithrombotic effect. Protein C also falls early, which is why heparin cover is used initially in acute thrombosis.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman with a pulmonary embolism is started on an unfractionated heparin infusion monitored with the APTT. How does heparin mainly produce its anticoagulant effect?
questions.e: Heparin binds antithrombin and greatly accelerates its inactivation of thrombin and factor Xa, which prolongs the APTT. Blocking vitamin K epoxide reductase is the action of warfarin, and conversion of plasminogen to plasmin is the action of thrombolytic agents.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has had three miscarriages in the second trimester and a deep vein thrombosis last year. Her APTT is prolonged and does not correct when her plasma is mixed with normal plasma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lupus anticoagulant, an antiphospholipid antibody, prolongs the phospholipid-dependent APTT in vitro and the inhibitor is not corrected by mixing, yet in vivo it causes thrombosis and pregnancy loss. A factor deficiency, such as factor XII deficiency, corrects when mixed with normal plasma.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy whose parents are cousins has recurrent nosebleeds and gum bleeding. Platelet count and morphology are normal. Platelet aggregation studies show no aggregation with ADP, collagen or adrenaline, but normal agglutination with ristocetin. Which platelet protein is defective?
questions.e: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor needed for platelet aggregation by all physiological agonists, while ristocetin-induced agglutination via GpIb remains normal. Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GpIb deficiency) shows the reverse pattern with giant platelets and a low count.

questions.s: A 7-year-old boy has a raised purpuric rash over the buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain, painful ankles and microscopic haematuria. Platelets are 320 x 10^9/L and PT and APTT are normal. What causes the purpura?
