questions.e: Palpable purpura with a normal platelet count, abdominal pain, arthritis and nephritis in a child is IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), in which IgA-containing complexes damage small vessels. Bleeding from thrombocytopenia gives flat petechiae, not palpable purpura.

questions.s: A 58-year-old man taking low-dose aspirin for ischaemic heart disease is scheduled for elective transurethral prostate surgery, and the surgeon asks him to stop aspirin seven days beforehand. Why is a week needed?
o: Synthesis of vitamin K-dependent factors falls
Fibrinolytic activity rises for a week
questions.e: Aspirin acetylates and permanently inactivates platelet cyclooxygenase-1, blocking thromboxane A2 for the life of the platelet; since platelets lack a nucleus, function recovers only as new platelets are released over 7-10 days. Aspirin does not affect vitamin K-dependent clotting factors at usual doses.

questions.s: A farmer in Sindh is bitten on the foot by a saw-scaled viper. Six hours later his gums are bleeding, and blood placed in a clean glass tube has not clotted after 20 minutes. What is the main mechanism of his coagulopathy?
o: Vitamin K antagonism by venom toxins
questions.e: Viper venoms contain procoagulant enzymes that activate clotting, consuming fibrinogen and other factors (venom-induced consumption coagulopathy), so the 20-minute whole blood clotting test shows incoagulable blood. This is corrected by antivenom, not by vitamin K.

questions.s: A 5-day-old boy bleeds persistently from the umbilical stump. Platelet count, PT, APTT and fibrinogen are all normal. Which test is most appropriate to identify the likely factor deficiency?
questions.e: Factor XIII cross-links fibrin to stabilise the clot; its deficiency causes umbilical stump bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage despite normal routine tests, because PT and APTT measure only clot formation. Clots lacking cross-links dissolve in 5 M urea, which is the screening test.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man has had central crushing chest pain for three hours. The ECG is non-diagnostic. Which blood test is most specific for myocardial injury?
questions.e: Cardiac troponins I and T are structural proteins specific to heart muscle, rising within hours and staying raised for days, so they are the preferred markers of myocardial injury. Myoglobin rises early but is also released from skeletal muscle, so it is not specific.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman has had profuse diarrhoea for four days and is clinically dehydrated. Creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.4 mg/dL. Urine sodium is 8 mmol/L and urine osmolality 650 mOsm/kg. What is the most likely cause of her acute kidney injury?
questions.e: In prerenal failure the tubules are intact and avidly conserve sodium and water, giving a low urine sodium (below 20 mmol/L) and concentrated urine. In acute tubular necrosis damaged tubules cannot reabsorb sodium or concentrate urine, so urine sodium is high and osmolality approaches that of plasma.

questions.s: A 19-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting and deep rapid breathing. Results: pH 7.10, PaCO2 20 mmHg, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L and chloride 98 mmol/L. How is this acid-base disturbance best described?
questions.e: Low pH and low bicarbonate indicate metabolic acidosis, the low PaCO2 is respiratory compensation (Kussmaul breathing), and the anion gap is 135 - (98 + 8) = 29, which is high because of ketoacids. A normal anion gap acidosis occurs with bicarbonate loss, as in diarrhoea.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man who feels well has a routine blood sample taken at a rural clinic; it reaches the laboratory the next day. Potassium is reported as 6.9 mmol/L and the laboratory notes the sample is haemolysed. His ECG is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Repeat the test on a promptly analysed sample
Start an insulin and dextrose infusion
questions.e: A delayed, haemolysed sample releases potassium from red cells, causing spurious hyperkalaemia; in a well patient with a normal ECG the result should be repeated on a fresh sample before treatment. Emergency treatment with calcium, insulin or dialysis is for true hyperkalaemia.

questions.s: A 65-year-old smoker with small cell lung carcinoma has a serum sodium of 122 mmol/L. He is clinically euvolaemic. Plasma osmolality is 255 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium 60 mmol/L; thyroid and adrenal function are normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Low plasma osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine and continued urinary sodium loss in a euvolaemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function is SIADH, here from ectopic ADH. In primary polydipsia ADH is suppressed and the urine is maximally dilute.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has painless progressive jaundice, pale stools, dark urine and a palpable gallbladder. Which pattern of liver tests is expected?
o: Raised unconjugated bilirubin with high urine urobilinogen
ALT over 1,000 U/L with only a mild ALP rise
Raised conjugated bilirubin with markedly raised ALP
questions.e: Biliary obstruction, here suggesting carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (with bilirubin in the urine) and a marked rise in ALP and GGT; urobilinogen is absent because bile does not reach the gut. Very high ALT points to hepatocellular injury such as viral hepatitis.

questions.s: A 20-year-old student notices yellow eyes on the third day of fasting in Ramadan. He is well. Bilirubin is 2.8 mg/dL, mostly unconjugated; ALT, ALP, haemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Gilbert syndrome is a common benign reduction in UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity, causing mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia that appears with fasting, illness or stress. Dubin-Johnson syndrome causes conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, and haemolysis is excluded by normal haemoglobin and reticulocytes.

questions.s: A 55-year-old woman has recurrent renal stones. Serum calcium is 11.6 mg/dL (8.5-10.5), phosphate 2.1 mg/dL (2.5-4.5) and parathyroid hormone is raised. Renal function is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: High calcium with a raised (not suppressed) PTH and low phosphate indicates primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from a parathyroid adenoma. In secondary hyperparathyroidism, as in chronic kidney disease, calcium is low or normal, and in malignancy and vitamin D toxicity PTH is suppressed.

questions.s: A 40-year-old woman has palpitations, weight loss and tremor. TSH is below 0.01 mU/L, free T4 is 1.5 ng/dL (0.8-1.8) and free T3 is markedly raised. What is the best description of these results?
questions.e: A suppressed TSH with raised free T3 but normal free T4 in a symptomatic patient is T3 toxicosis, seen early in Graves disease or with a toxic nodule. Subclinical hyperthyroidism has a suppressed TSH with both free T4 and free T3 normal, and secondary hyperthyroidism has an inappropriately normal or high TSH.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man has thickened Achilles tendons with xanthomas and a fasting LDL cholesterol of 290 mg/dL; triglycerides are normal. His father had a myocardial infarction at 40. Which defect is most likely?
questions.e: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is an autosomal dominant defect usually of the LDL receptor, so LDL is cleared poorly, causing very high LDL, tendon xanthomas and premature coronary disease. Lipoprotein lipase or apo C-II deficiency raises chylomicrons and triglycerides instead.

questions.s: A 45-year-old woman with known gallstones has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting for six hours. Which blood test is most useful to confirm the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Serum lipase (or amylase) above three times the upper limit of normal, with typical pain, confirms acute pancreatitis; lipase is more specific and stays raised longer. Serum calcium may fall in severe pancreatitis and helps assess severity but does not make the diagnosis.

questions.s: A 50-year-old overweight woman in Karachi has a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. Fasting plasma glucose is 92 mg/dL and the 2-hour value is 168 mg/dL. How should this be interpreted?
questions.e: A 2-hour value of 140-199 mg/dL with a normal fasting glucose is impaired glucose tolerance, a prediabetic state with a raised risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Diabetes requires a 2-hour value of 200 mg/dL or more, and impaired fasting glucose concerns the fasting value, which is normal here.

questions.s: A 5-week-old boy has had projectile, non-bilious vomiting after every feed for a week and is dehydrated. An olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. Which biochemical pattern is expected?
questions.e: In pyloric stenosis, vomiting of gastric acid loses hydrogen and chloride ions, and the kidneys exchange sodium for potassium and hydrogen to conserve volume, producing hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Acidosis appears only late in severe dehydration with poor perfusion.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man is rescued after 12 hours trapped under rubble with both legs crushed. He passes dark brown urine. Dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows no red cells. Which pigment is most likely in his urine?
questions.e: Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis; myoglobin released from muscle reacts with the haem-sensitive dipstick, yet no red cells are seen, and CK is very high. Haemoglobinuria gives the same dipstick result but would come with pink plasma, anaemia and evidence of haemolysis.

questions.s: Pus from a boil on the neck of a 30-year-old man shows Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters. The isolate is catalase positive and coagulase positive. What is the organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive are staphylococci, and coagulase positivity identifies Staphylococcus aureus, the commonest cause of boils. Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, and streptococci form chains and are catalase negative.

questions.s: Sputum from a 35-year-old man with a four-week cough is stained by the Ziehl-Neelsen method, and thin red bacilli are seen that keep the carbol fuchsin despite acid-alcohol treatment. Which component of the organism explains this?
o: Mycolic acid in the cell wall
questions.e: Mycobacteria have a waxy cell wall rich in mycolic acids, which holds the carbol fuchsin and resists decolorisation by acid-alcohol, making them acid-fast. A thick peptidoglycan layer explains Gram-positive staining, not acid-fastness.

questions.s: An 8-year-old boy in Karachi has had fever rising daily for five days, abdominal discomfort and a coated tongue. Typhoid fever is suspected. Which investigation is best to confirm the diagnosis at this stage?
questions.e: Salmonella Typhi is in the blood during the first week, so blood culture is the investigation of choice and also gives antibiotic susceptibility, which is vital with drug-resistant typhoid. The Widal test has poor sensitivity and specificity in endemic areas, and stool culture becomes positive later.

questions.s: A 6-year-old girl from Hyderabad, Sindh, has fever for eight days. Blood culture grows Salmonella Typhi resistant to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, co-trimoxazole, ciprofloxacin and ceftriaxone. She is well enough for oral treatment. To which oral antibiotic is such an isolate usually still susceptible?
questions.e: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid, which emerged in Sindh, resists first-line drugs, fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, but usually remains sensitive to azithromycin and carbapenems. Cefixime is a third-generation cephalosporin and is therefore ineffective against these strains.

questions.s: Reusable stainless steel surgical instruments at a district hospital must be made free of all microorganisms, including bacterial spores. Which method achieves this?
questions.e: Autoclaving, steam under pressure at 121 °C for about 15 minutes, kills all organisms including spores, so it sterilises heat-stable instruments. Boiling and alcohol kill vegetative bacteria but not reliably spores, so they only disinfect.

questions.s: An unvaccinated 5-year-old boy has fever, sore throat and a grey adherent membrane over the tonsils that bleeds when removed, with marked neck swelling. Two weeks later he develops myocarditis. How does the toxin responsible damage cells?
o: Blocks glycine release in the cord
Cleaves SNARE proteins at the NMJ
questions.e: Diphtheria toxin ADP-ribosylates elongation factor 2, halting protein synthesis in cells of the throat, heart and nerves, which causes the pseudomembrane, myocarditis and neuropathy. Raising cAMP via Gs is the action of cholera toxin.

questions.s: An 8-day-old baby delivered at home, whose cord was cut with an unclean blade, stops sucking and develops generalised muscle spasms with clenched jaw. The mother was not immunised. How does the responsible toxin cause these spasms?
o: Blocks release of glycine and GABA
Blocks acetylcholine release at the NMJ
questions.e: Tetanospasmin travels up motor nerves to the spinal cord and cleaves proteins needed to release the inhibitory transmitters glycine and GABA from Renshaw and other interneurons, causing spasms and rigidity. Blocking acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction is the action of botulinum toxin, which causes flaccid paralysis.

questions.s: A 26-year-old man has jaundice and ALT of 1,800 U/L. Serology shows HBsAg positive, IgM anti-HBc positive and anti-HBs negative. What is the most likely interpretation?
questions.e: HBsAg with IgM antibody to the core antigen indicates acute hepatitis B. Chronic infection shows HBsAg with IgG anti-HBc, and immunity from vaccination shows only anti-HBs because the vaccine contains surface antigen alone.

questions.s: A 25-year-old woman in Lahore in October has had high fever for two days with severe body aches and pain behind the eyes. Platelets are 140 x 10^9/L. Which test is most appropriate to confirm dengue at this stage?
questions.e: NS1 antigen circulates from the first day of fever for about five days, so it is the test of choice early in dengue. IgM antibodies usually appear only after about the fifth day, so an early negative IgM does not exclude dengue.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man from Bannu has fever and confusion. A thin blood film shows many red cells of normal size containing small delicate rings, some with two rings or double chromatin dots, and a few crescent-shaped gametocytes. Which species is present?
questions.e: Multiple fine ring forms in normal-sized red cells, high parasitaemia and banana-shaped gametocytes are typical of Plasmodium falciparum, which causes cerebral malaria. Plasmodium vivax enlarges the infected red cells and shows Schuffner dots and round gametocytes.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man dies with agitation and fear of water six weeks after being bitten by a stray dog; he received no vaccine. Brain histology shows round eosinophilic inclusions in the cytoplasm of hippocampal pyramidal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells. What are these inclusions?
questions.e: Negri bodies are cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions of rabies virus, found especially in hippocampal and Purkinje neurons. Cowdry type A bodies are intranuclear inclusions of herpes viruses, and Guarnieri bodies are seen in poxvirus infection.

questions.s: A 28-year-old man is tested three weeks after a high-risk exposure to HIV using a fourth-generation laboratory assay. What does this assay detect that allows earlier diagnosis than older antibody-only tests?
questions.e: Fourth-generation assays detect both p24 antigen, which appears early in acute infection, and HIV-1/2 antibodies, shortening the window period to around 2-6 weeks. Proviral DNA testing is used mainly for infants born to HIV-positive mothers, where maternal antibodies make antibody tests unhelpful.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has had foul-smelling, greasy diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss for three weeks. Fresh stool microscopy shows pear-shaped trophozoites with two nuclei and a falling-leaf motility. What is the organism?
questions.e: Giardia trophozoites are pear-shaped and binucleate, with a face-like appearance and falling-leaf motility; they attach to the small bowel mucosa and cause malabsorption with steatorrhoea. Entamoeba histolytica invades the colon and causes bloody dysentery.

questions.s: Cerebrospinal fluid is collected from a 2-year-old with suspected bacterial meningitis at a THQ hospital, for Gram stain and culture. How should the sample be handled before it reaches the laboratory?
o: Sent promptly, kept at room temperature
questions.e: Organisms such as Neisseria meningitidis and Haemophilus influenzae are fragile and die in the cold, so CSF for culture should reach the laboratory quickly without refrigeration. Formalin fixes and kills organisms, making culture impossible.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man with known rheumatic mitral valve disease develops low-grade fever, tiredness and splinter haemorrhages three weeks after a dental extraction. Echocardiography shows a small vegetation on the mitral valve. Which organism is most likely?
questions.e: Subacute endocarditis on a previously damaged valve after dental work is typically caused by viridans streptococci from the mouth, which have low virulence and cause an insidious illness. Staphylococcus aureus causes acute, destructive endocarditis, often on normal valves or in people who inject drugs.

questions.s: A 66-year-old man dies two days after an acute anterior myocardial infarction. What will histology of the infarcted myocardium most likely show?
questions.e: Between about 1 and 3 days, the infarct shows coagulative necrosis with loss of nuclei and a heavy neutrophil infiltrate. Macrophages clearing debris dominate at 3-7 days, granulation tissue at 1-2 weeks, and scar after several weeks.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man dies of pneumococcal lobar pneumonia on the third day of illness. The affected lobe is red, firm and airless, resembling liver, and the alveoli are packed with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin. Which stage is this?
questions.e: Red hepatisation (about days 2-4) is the stage of an exudate of neutrophils, red cells and fibrin filling the alveoli, giving a red liver-like consistency. In grey hepatisation the red cells break down, leaving a grey-brown fibrinous exudate.

questions.s: A 50-year-old man has nephrotic syndrome. Renal biopsy shows diffusely thickened capillary walls without hypercellularity, silver stain shows spikes projecting from the basement membrane, and antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor are present in serum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary membranous nephropathy, a common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, is due to subepithelial immune deposits, often with anti-PLA2R antibodies; basement membrane grows between them, producing spikes on silver stain. Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis shows hypercellularity and tram-track splitting of the basement membrane.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has been HBsAg positive for ten years. A liver biopsy shows scattered hepatocytes with abundant, finely granular, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm. What accounts for this appearance?
questions.e: Ground-glass hepatocytes in chronic hepatitis B have smooth endoplasmic reticulum distended with surface antigen, which can be shown with orcein stain or immunostaining. Clumped cytokeratin filaments are Mallory-Denk bodies, seen mainly in alcoholic liver disease.

questions.s: A 45-year-old man has dyspepsia. Antral biopsy shows chronic active gastritis with curved Gram-negative rods on the surface epithelium. Apart from gastric adenocarcinoma, long-standing infection with this organism is linked to which gastric neoplasm?
questions.e: Helicobacter pylori drives chronic antigenic stimulation of gastric lymphoid tissue, which can give rise to extranodal marginal zone (MALT) lymphoma; early lesions may regress after eradication therapy. Gastrointestinal stromal tumours arise from interstitial cells of Cajal and are not caused by H. pylori.

questions.s: A 50-year-old woman has itching and fatigue for a year. ALP is four times normal with normal ALT, ultrasound shows no duct dilatation, and anti-mitochondrial antibody is strongly positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary biliary cholangitis is autoimmune destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts in middle-aged women, with a cholestatic pattern and anti-mitochondrial antibodies in most patients. Primary sclerosing cholangitis affects larger ducts, is commoner in men with ulcerative colitis and shows beading on cholangiography.

questions.s: A 30-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule and an enlarged cervical lymph node. Fine-needle aspiration shows papillary clusters of cells with optically clear, overlapping nuclei, nuclear grooves and pseudo-inclusions, and occasional psammoma bodies. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed by its nuclear features (clear Orphan Annie nuclei, grooves and inclusions), often with psammoma bodies, and it spreads typically to cervical lymph nodes. Follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology because it needs capsular or vascular invasion, and it spreads by blood.

questions.s: A 35-year-old man has a thyroid nodule. FNA shows spindle and polygonal cells in an amyloid-rich stroma, and serum calcitonin is high. His brother had a phaeochromocytoma removed. Germline mutation of which gene is most likely?
questions.e: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells, and with a family history of phaeochromocytoma suggests MEN 2, caused by activating germline RET mutations. BRAF mutations are typical of sporadic papillary carcinoma, and PTEN of Cowden syndrome.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man wakes with a hot, red, extremely painful swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Joint aspirate shows needle-shaped crystals that are negatively birefringent under polarised light. What are the crystals?
questions.e: Acute gout is caused by monosodium urate crystals, which are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals of pseudogout are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, and usually affect the knee.

questions.s: In the classic adenoma-carcinoma sequence of sporadic colorectal cancer, loss of which gene typically occurs first, in normal mucosa or early adenoma?
questions.e: Loss of APC, a gatekeeper that controls beta-catenin, is the earliest step, followed by KRAS activation in growing adenomas and TP53 loss at the transition to carcinoma. Germline APC mutation causes familial adenomatous polyposis with hundreds of adenomas.

questions.s: Three days after an acute gastrointestinal bleed, a 50-year-old man's blood film shows many large, slightly blue-grey red cells (polychromasia). What are these cells?
questions.e: Polychromatic cells are young red cells (reticulocytes) still containing ribosomal RNA, released from the marrow in response to blood loss or haemolysis, and the response begins within a few days. Schistocytes are fragmented cells seen in microangiopathic haemolysis.

questions.s: A 26-year-old woman in the third trimester of pregnancy, with a poor diet, has haemoglobin 8.9 g/dL and MCV 112 fL. She has no neurological symptoms and her serum B12 is normal. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.e: Pregnancy greatly increases folate needs, and with a poor diet folate deficiency causes macrocytic megaloblastic anaemia; neurological signs are absent and B12 is normal. Iron deficiency, also common in pregnancy, causes microcytosis rather than macrocytosis.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has been on anti-tuberculosis treatment including isoniazid for four months without pyridoxine. He has microcytic anaemia with a raised ferritin. Bone marrow iron staining shows blue granules forming rings around erythroblast nuclei. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine, a cofactor for the first enzyme of haem synthesis, so iron accumulates in erythroblast mitochondria around the nucleus as ring sideroblasts, with high iron stores. Iron deficiency shows absent marrow iron.

questions.s: A 32-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops jaundice and anaemia. The film shows spherocytes and polychromasia and the reticulocyte count is 9 %. Which test will best confirm the cause of haemolysis?
questions.e: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, which can complicate SLE, is caused by IgG on red cells, detected by a positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test; partly phagocytosed cells become spherocytes. Osmotic fragility is increased with any spherocytes, so it cannot distinguish autoimmune haemolysis from hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man passes dark urine on waking, has pancytopenia and develops hepatic vein thrombosis. The direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which investigation will confirm the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria is an acquired PIG-A mutation in a stem cell, so cells lack GPI-anchored complement regulators CD55 and CD59, shown by flow cytometry; it causes complement-mediated haemolysis, thrombosis in unusual sites and marrow failure. Osmotic fragility tests membrane skeleton defects such as hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man has itching after hot baths, a ruddy face and splenomegaly. Haemoglobin is 19.5 g/dL with raised white cells and platelets, and serum erythropoietin is low. Which mutation is most likely?
questions.e: Polycythaemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm in which over 95 % of patients carry JAK2 mutations (mostly V617F), making red cell production independent of erythropoietin, which is therefore low. CALR and MPL mutations occur in essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis, and BCR-ABL1 defines CML.

questions.s: An 18-year-old student has fever, a sore throat, enlarged posterior cervical nodes and a palpable spleen. The film shows many large lymphocytes with abundant pale cytoplasm whose edges wrap around neighbouring red cells. What are these cells?
questions.e: In infectious mononucleosis, Epstein-Barr virus infects B cells, but the atypical lymphocytes seen on the film are mainly reactive cytotoxic CD8+ T cells responding to them. Lymphoblasts have scanty cytoplasm, fine chromatin and nucleoli, and would point to acute leukaemia.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man has lobar pneumonia. His white cell count is 19 x 10^9/L and the film shows many band forms, coarse dark granules in neutrophils and small blue cytoplasmic inclusions. How is this picture best described?
questions.e: Bacterial infection stimulates release of neutrophils, including immature band forms (left shift), with toxic granulation and Dohle bodies. Lymphocytosis is typical of viral infections and pertussis rather than pneumococcal pneumonia.

questions.s: A 52-year-old man has massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia with a very low monocyte count. Bone marrow aspiration is a dry tap. The film shows small lymphoid cells with fine hair-like cytoplasmic projections that are TRAP positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Hairy cell leukaemia is a B-cell neoplasm of middle-aged men with splenomegaly, pancytopenia, monocytopenia, a dry tap from marrow fibrosis, and TRAP-positive cells with hairy projections (usually with BRAF V600E). Myelofibrosis also gives a dry tap and splenomegaly but shows teardrop cells and a leucoerythroblastic film.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man had his spleen removed after a road accident. His blood film now shows small, round, dark purple inclusions in some red cells. What are these inclusions?
questions.e: Howell-Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants normally removed by the spleen, so they persist after splenectomy or in hyposplenism. Heinz bodies are denatured haemoglobin and need a supravital stain to be seen.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man arrives in haemorrhagic shock after a gunshot wound, and red cells are needed before his blood group can be determined. Which red cells are safest to give?
questions.e: Group O red cells carry neither A nor B antigen, so they are not destroyed by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B, and RhD-negative cells avoid sensitising RhD-negative recipients. AB is the universal donor group for plasma, not for red cells.

questions.s: A 6-year-old boy has recurrent bleeding into his knees and elbows. APTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing with normal plasma; PT and platelet count are normal and factor VIII level is normal. Deficiency of which factor is most likely?
questions.e: Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is X-linked factor IX deficiency, clinically identical to haemophilia A, with a prolonged APTT that corrects on mixing and a normal factor VIII. Factor XII deficiency prolongs the APTT but does not cause bleeding.

questions.s: A 12-year-old girl has lifelong nosebleeds and easy bruising. Platelets are 60 x 10^9/L and many are as large as red cells. Platelets do not agglutinate with ristocetin, and this is not corrected by adding normal plasma. Which protein is defective?
questions.e: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is deficiency of GpIb-IX-V, the platelet receptor for von Willebrand factor, giving giant platelets, mild thrombocytopenia and absent ristocetin agglutination that normal plasma does not correct. In von Willebrand disease ristocetin agglutination is corrected by normal plasma, which supplies the missing factor.

questions.s: A 65-year-old man receiving unfractionated heparin after hip replacement has a fall in platelets from 220 to 70 x 10^9/L on day 7 and develops a new deep vein thrombosis. What is the mechanism?
questions.e: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is caused by IgG antibodies against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin, which activate platelets, so thrombocytopenia occurs with paradoxical thrombosis 5-10 days after starting heparin. Dilutional thrombocytopenia follows massive fluid or blood replacement and does not cause thrombosis.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman taking warfarin for a mechanical heart valve attends the anticoagulation clinic. Which test is used to monitor her treatment?
questions.e: The prothrombin time tests the extrinsic and common pathways, which are sensitive to the fall in vitamin K-dependent factors, and the INR standardises it between laboratories for warfarin monitoring. The APTT is used for unfractionated heparin.

questions.s: A 55-year-old man with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C has a prolonged PT and low albumin. Which clotting factor is typically normal or even raised in liver disease, unlike the others?
questions.e: Factor VIII is made largely by sinusoidal endothelial cells outside hepatocytes and is an acute-phase protein, so its level is maintained or raised in liver disease. A low factor VIII in a patient with liver disease and bleeding suggests superimposed DIC.

questions.s: A raised D-dimer is found in a 45-year-old woman with suspected pulmonary embolism. D-dimer is a breakdown product of which substance?
questions.e: D-dimer is released when plasmin degrades fibrin that has been cross-linked by factor XIII, so it shows that clot has formed and been broken down. It is sensitive but not specific, so a normal value helps exclude thrombosis while a raised one has many causes.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man in Rawalpindi is on day 5 of dengue fever. His fever is settling but he has abdominal pain, his haematocrit has risen from 38 % to 48 % and platelets are 30 x 10^9/L. What does the rising haematocrit indicate?
o: Acute blood loss into the gut
questions.e: In the critical phase of dengue, around defervescence, increased capillary permeability lets plasma leak into serous cavities, concentrating the blood so the haematocrit rises; this warns of impending shock. Bleeding would cause haematocrit to fall, not rise.

questions.s: A 3-year-old boy had bloody diarrhoea a week ago. He is now pale and passing little urine. Haemoglobin is 6.5 g/dL with schistocytes, platelets 40 x 10^9/L and creatinine 2.8 mg/dL; PT and APTT are normal. What is the main mechanism?
questions.e: Typical haemolytic uraemic syndrome follows infection with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (or Shigella); the toxin damages glomerular endothelium, causing microthrombi, haemolysis with fragmented cells, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury. Autoantibodies to ADAMTS13 cause TTP, which is commoner in adults and less often dominated by renal failure.

questions.s: A 60-year-old man with obstructive jaundice from a pancreatic tumour has a prolonged PT before surgery. His platelet count is normal. What is the most likely cause of the prolonged PT?
o: Poor vitamin K absorption without bile
questions.e: Vitamin K is fat-soluble and needs bile salts for absorption, so biliary obstruction lowers factors II, VII, IX and X and prolongs the PT; it corrects within a day or two of parenteral vitamin K. An acquired factor VIII inhibitor prolongs the APTT, not the PT.

questions.s: Which bleeding pattern suggests a platelet disorder rather than a coagulation factor deficiency?
questions.e: Platelet disorders cause immediate mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, bruises, epistaxis, gum and menstrual bleeding. Haemarthroses, deep muscle haematomas and delayed bleeding are typical of clotting factor deficiencies such as haemophilia.

questions.s: A 25-year-old man has an extensive deep vein thrombosis. Despite increasing doses of unfractionated heparin, his APTT does not prolong as expected. His sister had a pulmonary embolism at 22. Inherited deficiency of which protein best explains this?
questions.e: Heparin works by potentiating antithrombin, so inherited antithrombin deficiency causes both venous thrombosis and relative resistance to heparin. Protein C and protein S deficiencies cause thrombophilia but do not reduce the response of the APTT to heparin.

questions.s: A 35-year-old woman has weakness, weight loss and darkening of the skin creases and buccal mucosa. Blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg, sodium 126 mmol/L and potassium 5.9 mmol/L. Which test will best confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) is confirmed by a failure of serum cortisol to rise after synthetic ACTH; the high ACTH causes pigmentation and aldosterone loss causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. The dexamethasone suppression test is used for suspected cortisol excess, not deficiency.

questions.s: A 38-year-old woman has central weight gain, purple abdominal striae, easy bruising and proximal muscle weakness. She takes no steroid medication. Which is an appropriate first screening test for her suspected condition?
questions.e: Endogenous Cushing syndrome is screened with tests of loss of normal cortisol control, such as failure of 1 mg overnight dexamethasone to suppress morning cortisol (or late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol). A random cortisol is unhelpful because of its normal diurnal and stress-related variation, and ACTH is measured only after cortisol excess is confirmed.

questions.s: A 68-year-old man with severe COPD is seen at a routine clinic visit and is clinically stable. Arterial gases on air: pH 7.36, PaCO2 60 mmHg, bicarbonate 33 mmol/L. How is this best interpreted?
o: Chronic respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
questions.e: A high PaCO2 with a slightly low pH points to primary respiratory acidosis, and the raised bicarbonate reflects renal retention over days, so the pH is nearly normal: chronic compensated respiratory acidosis. In primary metabolic alkalosis the pH would be above 7.40.

questions.s: A 4-year-old girl has had profuse watery diarrhoea for two days. Results: sodium 136 mmol/L, chloride 114 mmol/L, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, pH 7.24. What is the main mechanism of her acidosis?
questions.e: The anion gap is 136 - (114 + 12) = 10, which is normal, so this is a hyperchloraemic acidosis from loss of bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid. Ketoacidosis and lactic acidosis add unmeasured anions and raise the anion gap.

questions.s: Which serum enzyme is the most specific marker of hepatocellular injury?
questions.e: ALT is found mainly in the liver, so a raised ALT is relatively specific for hepatocyte injury. AST is also present in heart, skeletal muscle and red cells, and alkaline phosphatase rises mainly with cholestasis and bone disease.

questions.s: Two days after a total thyroidectomy, a 40-year-old woman has tingling around her mouth and twitching of the face when the facial nerve is tapped. Serum calcium is 7.1 mg/dL and phosphate is raised. What is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Removal or devascularisation of the parathyroid glands during thyroidectomy causes low PTH, giving hypocalcaemia with high phosphate because PTH normally promotes phosphate excretion. Vitamin D deficiency causes low calcium with low phosphate, as PTH rises in response.

questions.s: An 18-month-old boy from a family who keep him indoors has bowed legs, widened wrists and delayed walking. Which pattern of blood results is most likely?
o: High calcium, high phosphate, low ALP
Low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
Low phosphate, raised ALP, raised PTH
questions.e: In nutritional rickets from vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism keeps calcium low-normal while causing phosphate loss in the urine, and osteoblast activity raises alkaline phosphatase. Low calcium with high phosphate and low PTH describes hypoparathyroidism.

questions.s: A 30-year-old man passes 6 litres of dilute urine a day after a head injury. Plasma sodium is 148 mmol/L and urine osmolality 120 mOsm/kg after water deprivation; after desmopressin, urine osmolality rises to 600 mOsm/kg. What is the diagnosis?
questions.e: Inability to concentrate urine during water deprivation that corrects with desmopressin shows lack of ADH secretion, cranial diabetes insipidus, here from injury to the hypothalamus or posterior pituitary. In nephrogenic diabetes insipidus the kidneys do not respond to desmopressin, and in primary polydipsia urine concentrates with water deprivation.

questions.s: A 20-year-old man has fever, neck stiffness and a petechial rash. Which cerebrospinal fluid pattern is most typical of acute bacterial meningitis?
o: Lymphocytes, normal glucose, mildly raised protein
Lymphocytes, low glucose, very high protein, fibrin web
No cells, normal glucose, very high protein
questions.e: Acute bacterial meningitis produces a neutrophil-rich CSF with glucose consumed by bacteria and white cells and protein raised from a leaky blood-brain barrier. Lymphocytes with low glucose and very high protein suggest tuberculous meningitis, and lymphocytes with normal glucose suggest viral meningitis.

questions.s: A 28-year-old woman has had a complete hydatidiform mole evacuated. Which serum marker is used in her follow-up to detect persistent trophoblastic disease?
questions.e: Trophoblastic tissue secretes human chorionic gonadotrophin, so serial beta-hCG is followed until normal; a plateau or rise indicates persistent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. CA-125 is used mainly in epithelial ovarian cancer.

questions.s: A 14-year-old boy with beta-thalassaemia major has received monthly transfusions since infancy. Which blood test is used routinely to monitor his body iron load?
questions.e: Serum ferritin reflects total body iron stores and is checked regularly to guide iron chelation in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, along with MRI T2* of the heart and liver where available. Serum iron alone fluctuates widely and does not reflect stores.

questions.s: A 24-year-old man has a purulent urethral discharge and dysuria four days after unprotected sex. A Gram stain of the discharge shows Gram-negative kidney-shaped diplococci inside neutrophils. What is the organism?
questions.e: Intracellular Gram-negative diplococci in a male urethral discharge are diagnostic of gonorrhoea. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular organism that is not seen on Gram stain and usually causes a scantier discharge.

questions.s: CSF from a 65-year-old man with meningitis shows Gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci. On blood agar the colonies are alpha-haemolytic and are inhibited by an optochin disc. What is the organism?
questions.e: Streptococcus pneumoniae is an alpha-haemolytic, lancet-shaped diplococcus that is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, the commonest cause of bacterial meningitis in older adults. Viridans streptococci are also alpha-haemolytic but resist optochin.

questions.s: During a flood in Sindh, many people in a relief camp develop profuse painless rice-water diarrhoea and severe dehydration within hours. How does the toxin of the responsible organism cause the diarrhoea?
questions.e: Cholera toxin ADP-ribosylates the Gs protein, locking adenylate cyclase on; the rise in cAMP drives chloride and water secretion into the gut lumen without damaging the mucosa. Invasion and destruction of colonic mucosa is the mechanism of Shigella, which causes bloody dysentery.

questions.s: A cook at a hostel is linked to repeated cases of typhoid among students. She feels well, but Salmonella Typhi is isolated from her stool on several occasions over a year. Where does the organism most often persist in such chronic carriers?
questions.e: Chronic carriers usually harbour Salmonella Typhi in the gallbladder, often with gallstones, and shed it intermittently in stool. The organism multiplies in Peyer patches and the reticuloendothelial system during acute illness but rarely persists there.

questions.s: A 40-year-old man with a cough for five weeks has sputum sent from a district TB clinic. Which test detects Mycobacterium tuberculosis and rifampicin resistance directly from sputum within about two hours?
questions.e: Xpert MTB/RIF is an automated nucleic acid amplification test that detects M. tuberculosis DNA and the rpoB mutations causing rifampicin resistance in about two hours, and WHO recommends it as an initial diagnostic test. Culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium takes weeks, and skin tests and IGRAs show infection, not active disease.

questions.s: A 30-year-old blood donor is found to be anti-HCV antibody positive at screening. He feels well. What is the most appropriate test to determine whether he has current infection?
questions.e: Anti-HCV antibodies persist after both cleared and ongoing infection, so HCV RNA testing is needed to confirm active viraemia before treatment is considered. A normal ALT does not exclude chronic hepatitis C.

questions.s: During an outbreak linked to contaminated drinking water in a city, a 27-year-old woman in the third trimester of pregnancy develops jaundice, confusion and a prolonged prothrombin time. Which virus is most likely responsible?
questions.e: Hepatitis E is spread by the faecal-oral route, causes waterborne outbreaks in South Asia and carries a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure in late pregnancy. Hepatitis A is also waterborne but is not particularly severe in pregnancy.

questions.s: A 12-year-old boy from Khyber has a painless, crusted ulcerated nodule on his cheek for three months. A Giemsa-stained slit-skin smear from the edge shows many small oval bodies inside macrophages, each with a nucleus and a rod-shaped kinetoplast. What is the organism?
questions.e: Cutaneous leishmaniasis, common in north-west Pakistan, presents as a slowly growing painless ulcer on exposed skin, and smears show amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) with a nucleus and kinetoplast inside macrophages. Histoplasma yeasts in macrophages lack a kinetoplast.

questions.s: A 70-year-old man with Escherichia coli urosepsis develops fever, hypotension and DIC. Which component of the bacterium mainly triggers this host response by binding Toll-like receptor 4?
questions.e: Lipid A is the toxic part of lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin) in the Gram-negative outer membrane; it binds TLR4 on macrophages and endothelium, releasing TNF, IL-1 and other mediators that cause septic shock and DIC. Teichoic acid is a component of Gram-positive cell walls.

questions.s: A 5-year-old girl has intense itching around the anus that is worse at night and disturbs her sleep. Her brother has similar symptoms. Which test is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Enterobius vermicularis females lay eggs on the perianal skin at night, so eggs are best collected by pressing clear adhesive tape to the perianal skin on waking and examining it under the microscope. Eggs are seldom found in stool, so stool examination often misses the infection.

questions.s: A 70-year-old woman develops a low-grade infection of her prosthetic hip a year after surgery. Coagulase-negative staphylococci are grown from several samples. Which property of the organism best explains its ability to persist on the prosthesis despite antibiotics?
questions.e: Staphylococcus epidermidis produces an extracellular polysaccharide biofilm on plastic and metal implants, shielding bacteria from antibiotics and host defences, so infected prostheses often need removal. Coagulase and protein A are virulence factors of Staphylococcus aureus.
